title: Chapter 7: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
benchmark: Paul Krugman & Robin Wells, Macroeconomics (Principles SSOT, Spring 2027)

questions.title: Distinguishing Saving Flows from Wealth Stocks
questions.prompt_template: In macroeconomic accounting, what is the fundamental distinction between saving and wealth?

hints.text: Think of the bathtub analogy: water entering per minute versus the total water level at a given moment.
Saving is measured over a time interval (such as a month or year), whereas wealth is measured at a single point in time.

options_template.text: Saving is a stock variable measured at a point in time, whereas wealth is a flow variable measured per year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stock-Flow Reversal): This reverses the two definitions. Wealth is the accumulated stock at a point in time, while saving is the per-period flow.

options_template.text: Saving is a flow variable measuring unspent disposable income over a time period, whereas wealth is a stock variable measuring total net assets at a single point in time.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Saving (S = Y_d - C) is a flow over a period (like water flowing into a bathtub), and wealth (W) is the accumulated net stock of assets minus debts at a specific instant.

options_template.text: Saving includes only cash held in checking accounts, whereas wealth includes only physical real estate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asset-Category Confusion): Both saving flows and wealth stocks span all financial and physical assets; the distinction is temporal (flow vs. stock), not asset type.

options_template.text: Saving and wealth are identical whenever a household has zero debt.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Flow-Stock Equating): Even with zero debt, a household's annual saving flow is only the addition to its accumulated wealth stock, not the total stock itself.

questions.title: Capital Gains, Dissaving, and Wealth Evolution
questions.prompt_template: According to the stock-flow wealth accumulation identity W_t = W_{t-1} + S_t + Delta V_t, how can a household's net wealth decline during a year even though it saves a positive fraction of its paycheck?

hints.text: Look at the third term in the wealth accumulation equation beyond beginning wealth and active saving.
Wealth changes from both active saving (S_t) and asset valuation changes (Delta V_t, capital gains or losses).

options_template.text: It cannot decline; positive saving guarantees that end-of-year wealth strictly exceeds beginning-of-year wealth.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Valuation Changes): Active saving adds to wealth, but large capital losses on existing homes or stocks can more than offset positive saving.

options_template.text: Only if the household pays income taxes, which are subtracted after saving is computed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Disposable Income Order Error): Taxes are already deducted when computing disposable income (Y_d = Y + TR - T) before saving (S_t = Y_d - C) is calculated.

options_template.text: If capital losses on existing assets (Delta V_t < 0) are larger in magnitude than the household's positive saving flow (S_t > 0).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because W_t = W_{t-1} + S_t + Delta V_t, a drop in the market value of existing assets (such as a home or stock fund) can outweigh positive active saving and reduce net worth.

options_template.text: Only if the household converts bank deposits into government bonds.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Portfolio Reallocation Error): Exchanging one financial asset for another of equal market value changes portfolio composition, not total net wealth.

questions.title: Macroeconomic Physical Investment vs. Financial Investment
questions.prompt_template: Which of the following transactions counts as macroeconomic physical investment (I) in GDP rather than financial investment (household saving)?

hints.text: Ask whether the transaction creates newly produced physical capital that expands the economy's productive capacity.
Buying existing stocks or bonds merely transfers ownership of financial claims; physical investment requires new capital goods.

options_template.text: A logistics firm purchases newly manufactured electric delivery vans and builds a new distribution warehouse.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Spending on newly produced machinery, equipment, software, and commercial structures adds directly to the nation's physical capital stock (K) and counts as I in GDP.

options_template.text: A college professor buys $10,000 of shares of an existing technology corporation on the New York Stock Exchange.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial-as-Physical Investment): Purchasing shares on a secondary stock exchange transfers ownership of existing financial claims and counts as household saving, not physical investment.

options_template.text: A retiree purchases $25,000 of newly issued U.S. Treasury bonds through a brokerage account.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Bond-Purchase Misclassification): Buying government bonds is financial investment (supplying saving to the financial system), not spending on physical capital goods.

options_template.text: A household deposits $5,000 from its paycheck into a high-yield savings account at a commercial bank.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Saving-as-Investment Confusion): Depositing unspent income in a bank is household saving; physical investment occurs only if a borrower uses funds to buy new capital goods.

questions.title: New Residential Construction vs. Existing Home Purchases
questions.prompt_template: In National Income and Product Accounts (NIPA), how is a family's purchase of a newly constructed townhouse classified compared with a retiree's purchase of a 15-year-old condominium?

hints.text: Distinguish between newly produced structures that expand the housing stock and transfers of existing structures.
New residential construction is part of physical investment (I), whereas buying an existing home only transfers ownership.

options_template.text: Both purchases count as physical investment (I) because both involve residential real estate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Existing-Asset Inclusion): Only newly built housing adds to the economy's capital stock; reselling an existing home creates no new physical capital.

options_template.text: Both purchases count as household consumption (C) because families live in the homes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Housing-as-Consumption Error): In NIPA accounting, new residential construction is classified under physical investment (I), not consumption (C).

options_template.text: The existing condominium counts as physical investment (I), whereas the newly built townhouse counts as consumption (C).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Category Inversion): This reverses NIPA rules; new residential construction is I, while an existing home sale is an asset transfer excluded from current GDP investment.

options_template.text: The newly constructed townhouse counts as physical investment (I), whereas the 15-year-old condominium is an ownership transfer of existing housing stock that does not add to I.
options_template.feedback: Correct. New residential construction expands the nation's physical capital stock and is recorded in I, whereas buying an existing home transfers an already-produced asset.

questions.title: Defining Private Saving and Public Saving
questions.prompt_template: Using net taxes T_net = T - TR, how are private saving (S_p) and public saving (S_g) formally defined?

hints.text: Private saving is what households and firms retain from disposable income after consumption; public saving is the government's fiscal balance.
Check that when you add S_p and S_g together, T_net cancels out to leave national saving S = Y - C - G.

options_template.text: S_p = Y - C - G and S_g = T_net - C
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (National-vs-Private Saving Mixup): Y - C - G is total national saving (S), not private saving, and households—not the government—incur consumption C.

options_template.text: S_p = Y - T_net - C and S_g = T_net - G
options_template.feedback: Correct. Private saving equals disposable income (Y - T_net) minus consumption (C), and public saving equals net tax collections (T_net) minus government purchases (G).

options_template.text: S_p = Y + T_net - C and S_g = G - T_net
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Sign Reversal): Net taxes reduce private disposable income rather than adding to it, and public saving is revenue minus spending (T_net - G), not G - T_net.

options_template.text: S_p = Y - I - C and S_g = T_net + G
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Identity Misconstruction): Investment I is not subtracted to find private saving, and government purchases G reduce—rather than increase—public saving.

questions.title: Budget Deficits, Budget Surpluses, and National Saving
questions.prompt_template: When a government's purchases of goods and services exceed its net tax revenues (G > T_net), what is the resulting fiscal position and its direct accounting effect on national saving (S = S_p + S_g)?

hints.text: Evaluate the sign of public saving S_g = T_net - G when G > T_net.
A negative public saving balance reduces the sum S = S_p + S_g relative to private saving alone.

options_template.text: A budget surplus (S_g > 0), which increases national saving above private saving.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Deficit-Surplus Reversal): A surplus requires T_net > G; when G > T_net, the government spends more than it collects, creating a deficit.

options_template.text: A budget deficit (S_g < 0), which has no effect on national saving because private saving always offsets it dollar-for-dollar.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Assumed Full Offset): In national accounting, S = S_p + S_g; negative public saving directly subtracts from national saving unless private saving independently rises by the exact same amount.

options_template.text: A budget deficit (S_g < 0), which reduces national saving below the level of private saving.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When G > T_net, public saving is negative (a budget deficit), so national saving S = S_p + S_g is smaller than private saving S_p.

options_template.text: A balanced budget (S_g = 0), because the Treasury borrows the difference from bond markets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financing-as-Revenue Fallacy): Borrowing via bond issuance finances a deficit; it does not count as tax revenue and does not balance the budget.

questions.title: Open-Economy Investment Funding Identity
questions.prompt_template: In an open economy with net exports NX and net capital inflow NCI = -NX, which accounting identity links domestic physical investment (I) to domestic and foreign sources of saving?

hints.text: Start from Y = C + I + G + NX, rewrite Y - C - G as national saving S, and substitute NCI = -NX.
When an economy runs a trade deficit (NX < 0), foreign savers supply positive net capital inflows (NCI > 0) to help fund domestic investment.

options_template.text: I = S_p + S_g + NCI
options_template.feedback: Correct. Starting from Y - C - G = I + NX and substituting S = S_p + S_g and NCI = -NX yields I = S + NCI = S_p + S_g + NCI.

options_template.text: I = S_p + S_g - NCI
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Capital-Inflow Sign Error): Positive net capital inflows add to the pool of funds available for domestic investment rather than subtracting from it.

options_template.text: I = S_p - S_g + NX
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double Sign Error): National saving adds public saving (S_p + S_g), and net capital inflow is -NX rather than +NX.

options_template.text: I = S_p + S_g, regardless of whether NX is zero or nonzero
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Closed-Economy Generalization): I = S holds only in a closed economy (NX = 0); in an open economy, domestic investment can exceed or fall below national saving by NCI.

questions.title: Accounting Identities vs. Causal Mechanisms
questions.prompt_template: Why do macroeconomists emphasize that the open-economy identity S - I = NX does not by itself prove causation?

hints.text: Recall the distinction between an ex post accounting identity and a behavioral economic model.
An identity must always balance after the fact, but it cannot reveal which variable initiated the adjustment.

options_template.text: Because S - I = NX holds only in a closed economy where imports and exports are zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scope Error): In a closed economy NX = 0 so S = I; S - I = NX is specifically the open-economy accounting identity.

options_template.text: Because the identity frequently fails to hold during recessions when inventories accumulate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ex Post Identity Misunderstanding): Unplanned inventory changes are counted inside I, so the national accounting identity holds ex post in every period.

options_template.text: Because net exports depend exclusively on tariffs and are unrelated to saving or investment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade-Isolation Fallacy): Trade balances are tightly linked to saving, investment, and capital flows; the issue is identifying the direction of causation, not a lack of linkage.

options_template.text: Because it is an ex post accounting identity that always balances by definition and therefore requires a behavioral model to determine whether saving shifts or foreign asset demand drove the change.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Like 2 + 2 = 4, S - I = NX always holds by accounting definition; economists need behavioral models (like the loanable-funds market) to identify causal mechanisms.

questions.title: Distinguishing Bonds from Stocks as Financial Assets
questions.prompt_template: How does a corporate bond differ fundamentally from a share of corporate stock?

hints.text: Compare the legal claim held by a creditor versus a partial owner of a corporation.
One is a debt contract promising fixed payments; the other is an equity claim sharing in uncertain future profits.

options_template.text: A bond grants partial ownership and voting rights in the corporation, whereas a stock is a tradeable IOU promising fixed principal repayment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Debt-Equity Reversal): This swaps the definitions of stocks (equity ownership) and bonds (debt IOUs).

options_template.text: A bond is a tradeable debt IOU promising fixed interest payments and principal repayment at maturity, whereas a stock is a share of partial ownership in a corporation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Bondholders are lenders entitled to contracted interest and principal payments, while stockholders are partial owners entitled to a share of corporate profits.

options_template.text: Bonds can only be issued by governments, whereas stocks can only be issued by commercial banks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Issuer Restriction Error): Both governments and private corporations issue bonds, and corporations across all industries—not just banks—issue stock.

options_template.text: Bonds are classified as physical capital investment in GDP, whereas stocks are classified as consumption.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial-as-GDP Misclassification): Both bonds and stocks are financial assets; purchasing them on financial markets is household saving, neither I nor C.

questions.title: Identifying Financial Intermediaries
questions.prompt_template: Which group consists exclusively of financial intermediaries that gather funds from many individuals and transform them into diversified loans or asset portfolios?

hints.text: Distinguish institutions that pool saver funds indirectly from direct financial markets where securities trade.
Commercial banks, mutual funds, ETFs, pension funds, and life insurance companies are the canonical financial intermediaries.

options_template.text: The New York Stock Exchange and the U.S. Treasury bond auction market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direct-Market Confusion): Stock and bond markets are direct financial markets, not financial intermediaries.

options_template.text: Manufacturing corporations, software firms, and residential homebuilders.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Borrower-as-Intermediary Error): Nonfinancial firms are borrowers conducting physical investment, not financial intermediaries.

options_template.text: Commercial banks, mutual funds, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), pension funds, and life insurance companies.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Financial intermediaries pool funds from many savers and channel them indirectly into loans, bonds, and equities while lowering transaction costs and diversifying risk.

options_template.text: Zero-coupon Treasury bills, corporate bonds, and common stock certificates.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asset-vs-Institution Confusion): Bonds and stocks are financial assets (claims), not the intermediary institutions that pool and manage funds.

questions.topic: Three Core Tasks of the Financial System
questions.title: Core Macroeconomic Tasks of the Financial System
questions.prompt_template: Which list accurately states the three core macroeconomic tasks performed by a well-functioning financial system?

hints.text: Think about the three frictions that would prevent household savers from funding business investment directly.
Savers face search/contracting costs, firm-specific default risk, and the need for quick access to cash.

options_template.text: Reducing transaction costs, reducing risk through diversification, and providing liquidity.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Standardized markets and intermediaries cut contracting costs, pool funds across many borrowers to diversify idiosyncratic risk, and provide liquid access to cash.

options_template.text: Eliminating all macroeconomic risk, guaranteeing positive stock returns, and balancing the federal budget.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unrealistic-Guarantee Fallacy): Diversification removes firm-specific (idiosyncratic) risk, not economy-wide risk, and financial markets cannot guarantee positive returns or balanced budgets.

options_template.text: Printing currency, setting federal income tax rates, and directly building factories.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-and-Production Mixup): Fiscal taxation is Congress's role, currency issuance is the central bank's role, and nonfinancial firms build factories.

options_template.text: Maximizing household consumption, preventing foreign capital inflows, and fixing nominal interest rates at zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Antithetical Objectives): The financial system channels saving (not consumption), facilitates capital flows, and allows interest rates to allocate scarce funds.

questions.topic: Three Core Tasks of the Financial System
questions.title: Defining Financial Liquidity
questions.prompt_template: In macroeconomics and finance, what does it mean for an asset to have high liquidity?

hints.text: Consider how quickly and cheaply an asset can be turned into spendable cash during an emergency.
Compare a checking account deposit with a specialized factory machine or a suburban house.

options_template.text: The asset promises the highest possible long-run rate of return regardless of risk.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Return-as-Liquidity Confusion): Highly liquid assets (like checking deposits or T-bills) typically pay lower yields than illiquid long-term assets.

options_template.text: The asset is backed by physical machinery that cannot be sold for at least ten years.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Illiquidity Inversion): Physical capital locked up for years is illiquid; banks and secondary markets exist specifically to transform illiquid projects into liquid claims.

options_template.text: The asset's market price never changes when inflation or interest rates fluctuate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Stability-as-Liquidity Error): Secondary-market stocks and bonds are highly liquid even though their prices fluctuate daily.

options_template.text: The asset can be converted into spendable cash quickly without a significant loss of value.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Liquidity measures the ease, speed, and low cost of converting an asset into spendable cash—a key service provided by banks and secondary financial markets.

questions.title: Price in the Loanable-Funds Market and the Fisher Relationship
questions.prompt_template: What serves as the 'price' in the market for loanable funds, and how is it approximated by the Fisher equation?

hints.text: Borrowers and lenders care about inflation-adjusted purchasing power rather than purely nominal dollar returns.
Subtract expected inflation from the nominal interest rate.

options_template.text: The nominal interest rate (i), approximated as i approx r - pi^e.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal-Price & Sign Error): The loanable-funds market is priced in real terms (r), and the Fisher equation adds—not subtracts—expected inflation to obtain i (i approx r + pi^e).

options_template.text: The real interest rate (r), approximated as r approx i - pi^e.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because inflation erodes the purchasing power of repaid dollars, savers and investors evaluate the real interest rate r approx i - pi^e.

options_template.text: The real interest rate (r), approximated as r approx i + pi^e.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fisher Sign Reversal): Higher expected inflation reduces the real return on a given nominal rate, so pi^e must be subtracted from i, not added.

options_template.text: The Consumer Price Index (CPI), approximated as CPI approx i / pi^e.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Level Confusion): The CPI measures the aggregate price level of goods and services, not the intertemporal price of borrowing loanable funds.

questions.title: Reading Annual Saving Flows vs. Cumulative Wealth Trajectory
questions.prompt_template: In a stock-flow chart with zero capital gains (Delta V_t = 0), a household's annual saving bars fall from $10,000 in Year 2 to $8,000 in Year 3 and $7,000 in Year 4. How does the cumulative wealth line behave across Years 2, 3, and 4?

hints.text: Check whether the annual saving flows in Years 3 and 4 are still positive numbers.
As long as S_t > 0, each year's saving adds to the existing wealth stock W_{t-1}, even if the flow is smaller than the prior year.

options_template.text: The cumulative wealth line falls in Years 3 and 4 because annual saving decreased.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Confusing Falling Flow with Negative Flow): A smaller positive flow still adds water to the bathtub; wealth falls only when saving turns negative (dissaving) or capital losses exceed saving.

options_template.text: The cumulative wealth line stays completely flat after Year 2 until annual saving exceeds $10,000 again.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Threshold-Flow Fallacy): Wealth remains flat only when S_t = 0, not when S_t declines from one positive value to another.

options_template.text: The cumulative wealth line continues to rise in Years 3 and 4, though at a flatter (slower) slope than in Year 2.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because S_3 = +$8,000 and S_4 = +$7,000 are both positive flows, cumulative wealth keeps increasing, while the smaller annual increments make the wealth trajectory less steep.

options_template.text: The cumulative wealth line drops below the annual saving bars in Year 4.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stock-Below-Flow Impossibility): With nonnegative prior wealth and positive annual flows, cumulative wealth is the running sum and always lies at or above the current period's saving bar.

questions.title: Interpreting Open-Economy Funding Bars with Twin Deficits
questions.prompt_template: In a stacked bar diagram of an open economy running both a government budget deficit (S_g < 0) and a trade deficit (NX < 0), which two funding sources sit on the left bar to finance both domestic investment (I) and the government deficit (-S_g) on the right bar?

hints.text: Rearrange I = S_p + S_g + NCI by moving the budget deficit (-S_g > 0) to the uses-of-funds side.
I + (-S_g) = S_p + NCI, where NCI = -NX > 0.

options_template.text: Private saving (S_p) and positive net capital inflows (NCI = -NX > 0).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Rearranging I = S_p + S_g + NCI gives S_p + NCI = I + (-S_g): domestic private saving and foreign capital inflows jointly finance domestic investment and the public deficit.

options_template.text: Public saving (S_g) and positive net exports (NX > 0).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double Sign Reversal): With a budget deficit and a trade deficit, both S_g and NX are negative, so neither supplies funds to domestic investment.

options_template.text: Household consumption (C) and government purchases (G).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Spending-as-Saving Confusion): Consumption and government purchases absorb current output rather than supplying saving to fund capital formation.

options_template.text: Private saving (S_p) alone, because foreign capital inflows cannot finance government borrowing.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Closed-Capital-Market Fallacy): Foreign investors routinely purchase U.S. Treasury bonds as well as corporate securities, directly supplying NCI to domestic credit markets.

questions.title: Downward Slope of Investment Demand vs. Curve Shifts
questions.prompt_template: Why does the demand curve for loanable funds (I) slope downward when plotted with the real interest rate (r) on the vertical axis and loanable funds (Q) on the horizontal axis?

hints.text: Compare a capital project's expected rate of return against the real interest rate hurdle.
Lower real borrowing costs make more marginal investment projects profitable, causing a movement down along the demand curve.

options_template.text: Because a lower real interest rate shifts the entire investment demand curve rightward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift vs. Movement Confusion): A change in the vertical-axis price (r) causes a movement along the existing investment demand curve, not a shift of the curve.

options_template.text: Because firms undertake a physical capital project only if its expected rate of return is at least as high as r, so a lower r makes more projects profitable and increases the quantity of funds demanded.
options_template.feedback: Correct. As the real interest rate falls, additional factories, warehouses, and equipment projects clear the profitability hurdle, increasing Q_D along the downward-sloping demand curve.

options_template.text: Because households save less when the real interest rate falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-vs-Demand Mixup): Household saving behavior explains the upward slope of the supply of loanable funds (S), not the downward slope of investment demand (I).

options_template.text: Because government tax revenues fall whenever the real interest rate rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fiscal-Slope Confusion): The downward slope of investment demand reflects private firms' project hurdle rates, not automatic tax-revenue mechanics.

questions.title: Upward Slope of Loanable-Funds Supply
questions.prompt_template: On a loanable-funds graph, what causes a movement upward and to the right along a fixed supply curve (S)?

hints.text: Recall the rule separating movements along a curve from shifts of the curve.
Only a change in the real interest rate (r) produces a movement along a fixed supply curve of loanable funds.

options_template.text: A new federal tax credit for retirement accounts such as 401(k) and Roth IRA plans.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-as-Movement Error): Tax incentives that raise saving at every interest rate shift the entire supply curve rightward rather than moving along it.

options_template.text: A sudden increase in the federal government budget deficit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fiscal-Shift-as-Movement Error): A budget deficit reduces national saving at every interest rate, shifting the supply curve leftward.

options_template.text: A widespread cultural shift toward greater household thrift at every interest rate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Preference-Shift-as-Movement Error): Greater thrift at all interest rates shifts the entire supply curve rightward.

options_template.text: A higher real interest rate (r), which increases the reward for deferring current consumption and attracts additional foreign capital inflows.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A rise in r—the vertical-axis price—causes an upward-rightward movement along the existing upward-sloping supply curve, increasing the quantity of loanable funds supplied.

questions.title: Excess Supply Above the Equilibrium Real Interest Rate
questions.prompt_template: Suppose the market for loanable funds is currently at a real interest rate r_high that lies above the equilibrium rate r*. What condition appears on the graph, and how does the market adjust?

hints.text: At any vertical level above the intersection E*, compare the horizontal coordinate on the supply curve S to the coordinate on the demand curve I.
When Q_S > Q_D, lenders have unlent funds and compete by accepting lower real interest rates.

options_template.text: A surplus (excess supply) of loanable funds where Q_S > Q_D, putting downward pressure on r until r falls to r*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Above r*, desired saving exceeds desired investment; lenders lower interest rates to attract borrowers, reducing Q_S and raising Q_D until equilibrium is restored.

options_template.text: A shortage (excess demand) of loanable funds where Q_D > Q_S, driving r even higher.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Above-vs-Below Equilibrium Reversal): A shortage occurs below r*, not above r*; above equilibrium, supply exceeds demand.

options_template.text: A leftward shift of the supply curve S until equilibrium occurs at r_high.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Disequilibrium-as-Shift Fallacy): Market clearing from a disequilibrium interest rate occurs through movements along both curves as r falls, not by shifting S.

options_template.text: A permanent surplus because real interest rates cannot adjust downward in financial markets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sticky-Rate Assumption): In the loanable-funds model, r is flexible and adjusts downward whenever savers compete to lend surplus funds.

questions.title: Excess Demand Below the Equilibrium Real Interest Rate
questions.prompt_template: If the prevailing real interest rate is temporarily below the equilibrium rate r* in the market for loanable funds, what happens graphically as the market moves to equilibrium?

hints.text: Compare Q_D and Q_S at a horizontal slice below the intersection point E*.
Borrowers compete for scarce funds, bidding r up while moving up along both S and I.

options_template.text: Desired saving exceeds desired investment, so r falls until Q_S = Q_D.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Inversion): Below r*, investment demand exceeds saving supply (Q_D > Q_S), creating a shortage rather than a surplus.

options_template.text: The investment demand curve shifts leftward until the shortage disappears at the low interest rate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Instead-of-Movement Error): A shortage bids up the price r, causing movements along both curves rather than shifting the demand curve.

options_template.text: A shortage of loanable funds (Q_D > Q_S) bids the real interest rate upward, increasing Q_S along the supply curve and decreasing Q_D along the demand curve until they meet at E*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Competition among borrowers pushes r up toward r*, coaxing more saving along S and screening out lower-return projects along I.

options_template.text: Both the supply curve and the demand curve shift rightward simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Spurious Double-Shift Error): Disequilibrium at a non-clearing interest rate resolves via price adjustment along fixed curves, not simultaneous curve shifts.

questions.title: Effect of an AI Breakthrough or Investment Tax Credit
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a major breakthrough in artificial intelligence—or a new federal investment tax credit—raises the expected after-tax return on business capital projects at every real interest rate. How does the loanable-funds graph change, ceteris paribus?

hints.text: Determine whether improved business investment opportunities shift the demand curve I or the supply curve S.
Higher desired borrowing at every r shifts I rightward along an upward-sloping supply curve S.

options_template.text: The supply of loanable funds shifts rightward, lowering r* and raising Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Demand Curve Mixup): Business profitability and investment tax credits affect borrowers' demand for funds (I), not savers' supply curve (S).

options_template.text: The investment demand curve (I) shifts rightward, raising both the equilibrium real interest rate (r*) and the equilibrium quantity of loanable funds (Q*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Stronger expected returns increase borrowing demand at every r, shifting I right; the resulting shortage bids r* up and induces higher saving along S, raising Q*.

options_template.text: The investment demand curve (I) shifts leftward, lowering both r* and Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction-of-Shift Error): Better business opportunities and investment tax credits expand—rather than contract—investment demand.

options_template.text: The equilibrium quantity Q* increases while the real interest rate r* remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Horizontal-Supply Assumption): With an upward-sloping supply curve S, a rightward shift of I must raise r* to elicit the additional saving needed to fund higher Q*.

questions.title: Effect of Pessimistic Business Expectations
questions.prompt_template: If widespread business pessimism lowers the expected profitability of new factories and equipment at every real interest rate, what is the graphical impact on the loanable-funds equilibrium?

hints.text: Identify which curve shifts when firms cut desired borrowing at every r.
Trace the new intersection along the fixed upward-sloping supply curve S.

options_template.text: Supply shifts leftward, raising r* and lowering Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve Misidentification): Business investment expectations shift the investment demand curve (I), not the supply curve of loanable funds (S).

options_template.text: Demand shifts leftward, raising r* and lowering Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Direction Error): A leftward shift in demand creates a surplus at the old interest rate, pushing r* down, not up.

options_template.text: Supply shifts rightward, lowering r* and raising Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Curve & Quantity Error): Pessimism among corporate borrowers contracts investment demand (lowering Q*), rather than expanding saving supply.

options_template.text: Investment demand (I) shifts leftward, lowering both the equilibrium real interest rate (r*) and equilibrium investment (Q*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Reduced borrowing demand shifts I left along upward-sloping S, driving down both r* and equilibrium saving/investment Q*.

questions.title: Effect of Expanded Retirement Saving Incentives
questions.prompt_template: Suppose Congress expands tax advantages for 401(k) and Roth IRA accounts, encouraging households to save more at every real interest rate (holding the government budget balance constant). How does this shift the loanable-funds market?

hints.text: Identify whether household saving incentives shift S or I, and in which direction.
More saving at every r shifts S rightward along the downward-sloping investment demand curve I.

options_template.text: Loanable-funds supply (S) shifts rightward, lowering the equilibrium real interest rate (r*) and increasing equilibrium investment (Q*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher household saving shifts S right; the resulting surplus at the initial rate pushes r* down, encouraging firms to undertake more capital projects along I so Q* rises.

options_template.text: Loanable-funds supply (S) shifts leftward, raising r* and reducing Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Direction Reversal): Policies that encourage saving increase the supply of funds (rightward shift), not decrease it.

options_template.text: Investment demand (I) shifts rightward, raising both r* and Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Borrower-vs-Saver Mixup): Retirement saving incentives directly alter household saving supply (S), while firms' investment increases via a movement down along I.

options_template.text: Loanable-funds supply (S) shifts rightward, raising both r* and Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Price Sign Error): A rightward shift in supply creates a surplus of funds that pushes the equilibrium real interest rate down, not up.

questions.title: Graphical Mechanism of Government Budget Deficits and Crowding Out
questions.prompt_template: In the market for loanable funds where the supply curve represents national saving (S = S_p + S_g), how does a new government budget deficit cause crowding out?

hints.text: Remember that public saving S_g turns negative during a deficit, directly affecting national saving S.
Trace how the shift in S alters r* and induces a movement along the private investment demand curve I.

options_template.text: The investment demand curve shifts leftward, lowering r* and reducing private investment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Shift Misattribution): A budget deficit reduces national saving (shifting S left); private investment falls via a movement up along I as r* rises, not from a leftward shift of I.

options_template.text: The supply curve shifts rightward because the government prints new Treasury bonds, lowering r*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Bond-Supply Confusion): Issuing Treasury bonds means the government is borrowing from savers, which drains national saving available to private borrowers and shifts loanable-funds supply leftward.

options_template.text: The supply of loanable funds shifts leftward, raising the equilibrium real interest rate (r*) and causing a movement up and left along the investment demand curve (I) to a lower level of private investment.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A budget deficit lowers public saving (S_g < 0), shifting S left; the resulting higher r* prices marginal private investment projects out of the market (crowding out).

options_template.text: The supply curve shifts leftward, lowering r* and increasing private investment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Quantity Inversion): A leftward shift in supply creates a shortage at the old rate, which drives r* up and reduces—rather than increases—private investment.

questions.title: Graphical Decomposition of Partial Crowding Out
questions.prompt_template: On the loanable-funds diagram with an upward-sloping supply curve S_0 and downward-sloping demand curve I, a $50 billion government budget deficit shifts supply horizontally leftward by $50 billion to S_1. Why is the horizontal drop in equilibrium private investment (I_1* - I_2*) strictly smaller than $50 billion?

hints.text: Look at what happens to private saving along the original supply curve S_0 when r rises from r_1* to r_2*.
The deficit is split between reduced private investment and higher induced private saving.

options_template.text: Because the horizontal distance between S_0 and S_1 shrinks as the interest rate rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Parallel-Shift Misreading): A lump-sum $50B deficit shifts S leftward by exactly $50B at every interest rate; the gap between parallel curves does not shrink.

options_template.text: Because the higher equilibrium real interest rate (r_2* > r_1*) induces households to supply additional private saving along the upward-sloping supply curve, absorbing part of the $50 billion deficit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because S slopes upward, the higher r_2* coaxes extra private saving (Delta S_p > 0), so private investment falls by less than the full deficit (|Delta I| < $50B).

options_template.text: Because the investment demand curve automatically shifts rightward to offset the deficit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Spurious Demand Offset): A budget deficit does not shift the private investment demand curve rightward; firms simply move upward along a fixed I curve.

options_template.text: Because a $50 billion deficit always reduces private investment by more than $50 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Over-Crowding Error): With downward-sloping I and upward-sloping S, |Delta I| is strictly less than the deficit (partial crowding out), never greater than it.

questions.title: Comparing Vertical, Upward-Sloping, and Flat Supply Regimes
questions.prompt_template: In a three-panel comparison of crowding-out regimes in the loanable-funds market, which slope of the supply curve (S) generates complete one-for-one crowding out (Delta I = -Delta Deficit)?

hints.text: Complete crowding out occurs when a higher real interest rate induces zero additional private saving or foreign capital inflow.
Which geometric line has zero response of quantity supplied to changes in the vertical-axis real interest rate?

options_template.text: A horizontal (perfectly elastic) supply curve, where Delta r approx 0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity-Regime Reversal): A flat/elastic supply curve (as during recessionary slack with monetary accommodation) yields nearly zero crowding out (Delta I approx 0), not complete crowding out.

options_template.text: An upward-sloping supply curve with moderate elasticity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Partial-vs-Complete Confusion): An upward-sloping supply curve produces partial crowding out (|Delta I| < Delta Deficit) because higher r induces extra saving.

options_template.text: A downward-sloping supply curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Invalid Supply Slope): The standard loanable-funds supply curve does not slope downward in the three crowding-out regimes.

options_template.text: A vertical (perfectly inelastic) supply curve, where private saving does not respond at all to higher real interest rates.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When S is vertical, the fixed pool of saving cannot expand as r rises, so every dollar of government deficit displaces a full dollar of private investment (Delta I = -Delta Deficit).

questions.title: Simultaneous Budget Deficit and AI Investment Boom
questions.prompt_template: Suppose two events occur simultaneously in the loanable-funds market: (1) the federal government runs a large budget deficit, and (2) an AI data-center boom increases private investment demand at every real interest rate. What is the unambiguous graphical prediction?

hints.text: Sketch both shifts: S shifts leftward, and I shifts rightward.
Check whether both shifts push r* in the same direction and whether they pull Q* in opposite directions.

options_template.text: The equilibrium real interest rate (r*) unambiguously rises, while the change in equilibrium quantity (Q*) is ambiguous without knowing the relative sizes of the two shifts.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Both a leftward shift of S (deficit) and a rightward shift of I (investment boom) push r* upward, whereas the deficit lowers Q* and the investment boom raises Q*.

options_template.text: The equilibrium quantity (Q*) unambiguously rises, while the change in the real interest rate (r*) is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ambiguous-Variable Swap): Here r* moves in the same direction (up) under both shocks, while Q* is pulled in opposite directions.

options_template.text: Both r* and Q* unambiguously fall.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong-Direction Synthesis): Neither a budget deficit nor an investment boom reduces r*; both raise borrowing costs.

options_template.text: Both r* and Q* remain completely unchanged because the two shifts cancel out.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Spurious Cancellation): Leftward S and rightward I reinforce each other's upward effect on r*; they do not cancel out on the interest rate.

questions.title: Calculating Household Saving Flow from Gross Income, Transfers, and Taxes
questions.prompt_template: During a year, a household earns $100,000 in gross income (Y), receives $4,000 in government transfers (TR), pays $24,000 in taxes (T), and spends $68,000 on consumption (C). What is the household's annual saving flow (S)?

hints.text: First compute disposable income Y_d = Y + TR - T before subtracting consumption.
Substitute Y_d = $100,000 + $4,000 - $24,000 = $80,000, then calculate S = Y_d - C.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Transfers): Subtracting taxes from gross income without adding $4,000 in transfers gives Y_d = $76,000 and S = $8,000.
Diagnostic fallacy (Transfer Sign Error): Subtracting transfers instead of adding them yields Y_d = $72,000 and S = $4,000.
Correct. Disposable income is Y_d = $100,000 + $4,000 - $24,000 = $80,000, so the annual saving flow is S = $80,000 - $68,000 = $12,000 (a 15.0% personal saving rate).
Diagnostic fallacy (Gross-Income Confusion): Computing Y - C = $100,000 - $68,000 ignores both taxes and transfers.

questions.title: Computing End-of-Year Wealth with Saving and a Capital Loss
questions.prompt_template: A household starts the year with $150,000 in net wealth (W_0). During the year, it earns $90,000 in disposable income (Y_d), spends $76,000 on consumption (C), and suffers a $9,000 capital loss (Delta V_1 = -$9,000) on its existing stock index fund. What is its end-of-year wealth stock (W_1)?

hints.text: Compute the annual saving flow S_1 = Y_d - C first, then apply W_1 = W_0 + S_1 + Delta V_1.
Remember that a capital loss enters Delta V_1 with a negative sign.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Capital Loss): Adding S_1 = $14,000 to $150,000 while ignoring the -$9,000 capital loss overstates ending wealth.
Diagnostic fallacy (Capital-Loss Sign Reversal): Adding +$9,000 instead of subtracting $9,000 treats a capital loss as a capital gain.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Saving Flow): Subtracting the $9,000 capital loss from $150,000 while forgetting to add the $14,000 saving flow understates ending wealth.

questions.title: Decomposing Private Saving, Public Saving, and Investment in a Closed Economy
questions.prompt_template: In a closed economy (NX = 0), GDP is Y = $12,000 billion, consumption is C = $7,800 billion, government purchases are G = $2,400 billion, and net taxes are T_net = $2,100 billion. What are private saving (S_p), public saving (S_g), and domestic investment (I)?

hints.text: Apply S_p = Y - T_net - C, S_g = T_net - G, and the closed-economy identity I = S_p + S_g.
Check that S_p + S_g equals Y - C - G = $12,000B - $7,800B - $2,400B.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Public-Saving Sign Reversal): Computing G - T_net instead of T_net - G mistakenly turns a $300B budget deficit into a surplus.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Net Taxes in Private Saving): Computing Y - C instead of Y - T_net - C forgets to subtract $2,100B in net taxes from private income.
Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Budget Deficit in National Saving): Setting I = S_p ignores the -$300B government deficit that reduces national saving to $1,800B.

questions.title: Computing Net Capital Inflow and Net Exports in an Open Economy
questions.prompt_template: An open economy has GDP Y = $18,000 billion, consumption C = $12,200 billion, government purchases G = $3,200 billion, net taxes T_net = $2,900 billion, and domestic physical investment I = $3,100 billion. What are net capital inflow (NCI) and net exports (NX)?

hints.text: First find national saving S = Y - C - G (or S_p + S_g), then use I = S + NCI.
Once you find NCI = I - S, apply NX = -NCI.

options_template.text: NCI = -$500 billion and NX = +$500 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (NCI-NX Sign Reversal): Because domestic investment ($3,100B) exceeds national saving ($2,600B), the economy must borrow $500B from abroad (NCI = +$500B, NX = -$500B).

options_template.text: NCI = +$500 billion and NX = -$500 billion
NCI = +$200 billion and NX = -$200 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Using Private Saving Instead of National Saving): Computing I - S_p = 3,100 - 2,900 = +$200B omits the -$300B government budget deficit.

options_template.text: NCI = +$800 billion and NX = -$800 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting the Deficit): Subtracting the $300B deficit twice from national saving overstates NCI by $300B.

questions.title: Inverse Bond Price Adjustment When Market Yields Rise
questions.prompt_template: A one-year zero-coupon bond has a face value of F = $1,092. Initially, the market nominal interest rate is i_1 = 4.0%, so the bond trades at P_{B,1} = $1,050. If market interest rates rise to i_2 = 5.0%, what is the bond's new market price P_{B,2}?

hints.text: Use the zero-coupon bond pricing formula P_B = F / (1 + i).
Divide $1,092 by 1.05 rather than multiplying by 0.95 or 1.05.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direct-Relationship Error): Bond prices move inversely—not positively—with market interest rates; a higher yield lowers the price of an existing bond.
Diagnostic fallacy (Discount-Multiplication Shortcut): Multiplying $1,092 by (1 - 0.05) = 0.95 instead of dividing by 1.05 understates the bond's present value.
Correct. Using P_{B,2} = F / (1 + i_2) = $1,092 / 1.05 = $1,040.00, the bond's price falls by $10 so a new buyer earns exactly a 5.0% yield ($52 / $1,040 = 0.05).
Diagnostic fallacy (Compounding Instead of Discounting): Multiplying $1,092 by 1.05 compounds forward rather than discounting the future face value to today.

questions.title: Exact Fisher Equation Calculation of the Real Interest Rate
questions.prompt_template: A one-year bond pays a nominal interest rate of i = 7.1% when expected inflation is pi^e = 2.0%. Using the exact Fisher formula 1 + r = (1 + i) / (1 + pi^e), what is the exact expected real interest rate (r)?

hints.text: Convert percentages to decimals (i = 0.071, pi^e = 0.020) before dividing (1 + i) by (1 + pi^e).
Compute 1.071 / 1.020 and then subtract 1.

options_template.feedback: Correct. By the exact Fisher equation, 1 + r = 1.071 / 1.020 = 1.05, so r = 0.05, or exactly 5.0%.
Diagnostic fallacy (Approximation Used Instead of Exact Formula): Subtracting 7.1% - 2.0% = 5.1% gives the linear approximation rather than the exact Fisher formula requested.
Diagnostic fallacy (Adding Expected Inflation): Adding i + pi^e = 7.1% + 2.0% moves in the wrong direction; inflation erodes real returns.
Diagnostic fallacy (Raw Ratio Error): Dividing 7.1% directly by 2.0% instead of computing (1 + i) / (1 + pi^e) - 1 violates the Fisher identity.

questions.title: Portfolio Volatility Reduction Through Diversification
questions.prompt_template: Suppose each independent clean-energy startup has an annual return standard deviation of sigma = 32%. If an equally weighted mutual fund invests in N = 64 uncorrelated startups, what is the portfolio's return standard deviation (sigma_p = sigma / sqrt(N))?

hints.text: Take the square root of the number of uncorrelated assets N before dividing sigma.
Since sqrt(64) = 8, divide 32% by 8.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dividing by N Instead of sqrt(N)): Computing 32% / 64 = 0.5% overstates risk reduction because portfolio standard deviation scales with 1 / sqrt(N), not 1 / N.
Diagnostic fallacy (Halving Heuristic): Dividing 32% by 2 fails to apply the square-root diversification formula for 64 independent assets.
Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Diversification): Assuming portfolio volatility stays at 32% treats uncorrelated startups as if they were perfectly correlated.
Correct. Using sigma_p = sigma / sqrt(N) = 32% / sqrt(64) = 32% / 8 = 4.0%, pooling 64 uncorrelated firms slashes idiosyncratic volatility by a factor of 8.

questions.title: Solving for Equilibrium Real Interest Rate and Loanable Funds
questions.prompt_template: In the market for loanable funds, supply is Q_S = -60 + 40r and investment demand is Q_D = 240 - 20r (where Q is in billions of dollars and r is in percentage points). What are the equilibrium real interest rate (r*) and equilibrium quantity of loanable funds (Q*)?

hints.text: Set Q_S = Q_D and collect all r terms on one side and constants on the other.
Solve -60 + 40r* = 240 - 20r* for r*, then substitute r* back into either equation.

options_template.text: r* = 3.0% and Q* = $180 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Sign Error): Subtracting 60 from 240 (60r = 180) instead of adding 60 to both sides yields r = 3.0%.

options_template.text: r* = 5.0% and Q* = $140 billion
r* = 9.0% and Q* = $60 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-and-Intercept Sign Errors): Computing (40 - 20)r = 240 - 60 gives 20r = 180 and r = 9.0%.

options_template.text: r* = 5.0% and Q* = $200 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Supply Intercept): Plugging r* = 5.0% into 40r = 200 while forgetting the -60 intercept in Q_S = -60 + 40r overstates Q* by $60B.

questions.title: Quantifying a Surplus of Loanable Funds Above Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: Using the loanable-funds market Q_S = -60 + 40r and Q_D = 240 - 20r (where equilibrium is r* = 5.0%), what disequilibrium exists if the real interest rate is temporarily r = 6.5%?

hints.text: Evaluate both Q_S and Q_D at r = 6.5% and compare them.
Since r = 6.5% is above r* = 5.0%, Q_S will exceed Q_D, creating a surplus equal to Q_S - Q_D.

options_template.text: A shortage of $90 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Reversal): At r = 6.5%, Q_S ($200B) exceeds Q_D ($110B), which is a surplus (excess supply), not a shortage.

options_template.text: A surplus of $150 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Supply Intercept): Evaluating Q_S as 40(6.5) = $260B without subtracting 60 inflates the calculated surplus by $60B.

options_template.text: A surplus of $90 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. At r = 6.5%, Q_S = -60 + 40(6.5) = $200B and Q_D = 240 - 20(6.5) = $110B, producing an excess supply (surplus) of $200B - $110B = $90 billion.

options_template.text: A shortage of $60 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong-Side Rate Evaluation): A $60B shortage occurs below equilibrium at r = 4.0% (where Q_S = $100B and Q_D = $160B), not at r = 6.5%.

questions.title: New Equilibrium After a Rightward Investment Demand Shift
questions.prompt_template: Initially, loanable-funds supply is Q_S = -30 + 30r and investment demand is Q_{D,0} = 210 - 30r (with initial equilibrium r_1* = 4.0% and Q_1* = $90 billion). An investment tax credit increases investment demand by $60 billion at every real interest rate, giving Q_{D,1} = 270 - 30r. What are the new equilibrium real interest rate (r_2*) and quantity (Q_2*)?

hints.text: Equate the unchanged supply curve Q_S = -30 + 30r to the new demand curve Q_{D,1} = 270 - 30r.
Solve 60r_2* = 300 for r_2*, then substitute into Q_{D,1} to find Q_2*.

options_template.text: r_2* = 5.0% and Q_2* = $120 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting -30 + 30r_2* = 270 - 30r_2* gives 60r_2* = 300, so r_2* = 5.0% and Q_2* = 270 - 30(5.0) = $120 billion (+$30B net increase).

options_template.text: r_2* = 5.0% and Q_2* = $150 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Shift Quantity Error): Adding the entire $60B horizontal shift to $90B ignores that the higher interest rate (5.0% vs. 4.0%) dampens part of the investment increase.

options_template.text: r_2* = 3.0% and Q_2* = $120 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shifting Supply Instead of Demand): Lowering r* to 3.0% reflects a +$60B rightward shift in saving supply, not investment demand.

options_template.text: r_2* = 4.0% and Q_2* = $150 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Interest-Rate Fallacy): Holding r* fixed at 4.0% ignores the shortage created by the demand shift that bids r* up to 5.0%.

questions.title: Calculating Crowded-Out Private Investment from a Budget Deficit
questions.prompt_template: Baseline loanable-funds supply is Q_{S,0} = -40 + 50r and investment demand is Q_D = 260 - 25r (so initially r_1* = 4.0% and I_1* = $160 billion). A $75 billion government budget deficit shifts supply leftward by $75 billion to Q_{S,1} = -115 + 50r. By how much is private investment crowded out?

hints.text: Solve for the new equilibrium r_2* and I_2* using Q_{S,1} = Q_D.
Compare I_2* against initial investment I_1* = $160 billion to find the crowded-out amount.

options_template.text: $75 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Complete Crowding-Out Assumption): Assuming private investment falls by the entire $75B deficit ignores the +$50B in extra private saving induced by the higher interest rate.

options_template.text: $50 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Swapping Induced Saving and Crowded-Out Investment): $50 billion is the increase in private saving (from $160B to $210B along Q_{S,0}), not the fall in private investment.

options_template.text: $0 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero Crowding-Out Assumption): Because investment demand slopes downward and r* rises from 4.0% to 5.0%, private investment must decline.

options_template.text: $25 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Equating -115 + 50r_2* = 260 - 25r_2* gives 75r_2* = 375, so r_2* = 5.0% and I_2* = 260 - 25(5.0) = $135B. Private investment falls by $160B - $135B = $25 billion.

questions.title: Decomposing How a $50 Billion Budget Deficit Is Financed
questions.prompt_template: Suppose initial loanable-funds supply is Q_{S,0} = -20 + 60r and investment demand is Q_D = 280 - 40r (initial equilibrium: r_1* = 3.0%, I_1* = $160 billion). A $50 billion government budget deficit shifts supply to Q_{S,1} = -70 + 60r. How is the $50 billion deficit financed between induced private saving (Delta S_p) and crowded-out private investment (Delta I)?

hints.text: Find r_2* and I_2* from Q_{S,1} = Q_D, then evaluate private saving along the original curve Q_{S,0} at r_2*.
Verify your two components satisfy Delta S_p + |Delta I| = $50 billion.

options_template.text: +$20 billion in induced private saving and -$30 billion in crowded-out private investment
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Component Swap): This swaps the two magnitudes; because supply is steeper in quantity response (slope 60 vs. 40), induced saving absorbs the larger share (+$30B) and investment falls by -$20B.

options_template.text: +$30 billion in induced private saving and -$20 billion in crowded-out private investment
$0 billion in induced private saving and -$50 billion in crowded-out private investment
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Complete Crowding-Out Fallacy): This would hold only if supply were vertical (zero response to r), not Q_{S,0} = -20 + 60r.

options_template.text: +$50 billion in induced private saving and $0 billion in crowded-out private investment
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero Crowding-Out Fallacy): Because r* rises by 0.5 percentage points along downward-sloping investment demand, private investment falls by 40(0.5) = $20B.

questions.title: Coexistence of Large U.S. Deficits and Record AI Data-Center Investment (2023-2026)
questions.prompt_template: Between 2023 and 2026, U.S. federal budget deficits exceeded $1.6 trillion annually, yet technology and utility firms still financed hundreds of billions of dollars in hyperscale AI data centers and grid upgrades. Which macroeconomic mechanism best explains how both occurred simultaneously?

hints.text: Think about both open-economy capital flows and how high-expected-return projects respond to higher real interest rates.
Partial crowding out leaves room for top-return investments when higher yields attract domestic saving and foreign capital inflows.

options_template.text: Budget deficits have zero effect on real interest rates in any full-employment economy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Blanket Deficit-Neutrality Fallacy): At full employment, structural deficits do push up real interest rates (as seen in rising TIPS yields) and crowd out more rate-sensitive sectors.

options_template.text: AI data centers do not count as physical investment, so they do not compete in the loanable-funds market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Capital-Classification Error): Cloud servers, semiconductor fabs, and grid upgrades are core physical capital investment (I) funded through capital markets.

options_template.text: Higher real interest rates attracted additional domestic saving and large foreign capital inflows (NCI > 0) that cushioned crowding out, while high expected returns on AI infrastructure cleared the steeper borrowing hurdle.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Open-economy capital inflows and induced private saving prevented 1-for-1 crowding out, while high-return AI projects outcompeted lower-return projects at higher real yields.

options_template.text: The United States ran large trade surpluses (NX > 0) during 2023-2026, exporting saving to foreign borrowers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade-Balance Inversion): Financing investment above national saving requires foreign capital inflows (NCI > 0), which correspond to a trade deficit (NX < 0), not a surplus.

questions.title: Rebuilding Depleted Wealth During the 2007-2009 Great Recession
questions.prompt_template: In BEA data (FRED: PSAVERT), the U.S. personal saving rate jumped from roughly 2.5% in 2007 to over 6% by 2009 despite falling incomes. Using the wealth accumulation identity W_t = W_{t-1} + S_t + Delta V_t, what best explains this surge in saving?

hints.text: Consider what happened to home prices and equity portfolios (Delta V_t) during the 2007-2009 financial crisis.
When capital losses erase wealth, households often raise active saving flows S_t to restore target wealth buffers.

options_template.text: Collapsing home and stock prices generated massive capital losses (Delta V_t < 0), prompting households to cut discretionary consumption and raise saving flows (S_t) to rebuild depleted wealth buffers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Sharp balance-sheet losses in housing and equities reduced household net worth, inducing families to save a larger share of disposable income to repair their wealth stock.

options_template.text: Rising home prices produced huge capital gains, forcing households to save more out of every paycheck.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Historical & Behavioral Inversion): Home prices collapsed rather than rose in 2007-2009, and positive capital gains typically encourage higher consumption rather than higher active saving.

options_template.text: The personal saving rate rose automatically because PSAVERT includes capital gains in its numerator.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (NIPA Definition Error): PSAVERT measures active saving flows (Y_d - C) as a share of disposable income and excludes capital gains or losses on existing assets.

options_template.text: Higher real interest rates above 10% in 2009 induced households to postpone consumption.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Historical Rate Error): Real interest rates fell below 1% during the 2009 recession rather than spiking above 10%.

questions.title: 2020 Pandemic Saving Spike and Subsequent 'Excess Savings' Spend-Down
questions.prompt_template: In April 2020, the U.S. personal saving rate (FRED: PSAVERT) spiked above 30% before normalizing near 4%-5% in 2024-2026. How does the stock-flow framework explain why that temporary 2020 flow spike continued to boost consumer spending through 2022-2023?

hints.text: Distinguish between a temporary jump in the saving flow (S_t) and the resulting accumulated wealth stock (W_t).
High saving flows during lockdowns accumulated into a large stock of liquid balances that households could later draw down.

options_template.text: Because once a saving flow rises in one month, it is legally locked in at 30% for the next three years.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Flow-Persistence Fallacy): Saving flows fell back rapidly after lockdowns ended; what persisted was the accumulated stock of liquid wealth.

options_template.text: Because pandemic stimulus transfers are classified as physical investment (I) rather than disposable income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (NIPA Transfer Misclassification): Government transfers (TR) raise household disposable income (Y_d = Y + TR - T), not physical investment.

options_template.text: Because closed restaurants reduced household wealth, forcing families to spend more in 2022.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal on Wealth): Forced reductions in spending alongside stimulus transfers raised—not reduced—household liquid wealth.

options_template.text: Stimulus transfers combined with lockdown spending restrictions created huge positive saving flows (S_t) that accumulated into a stock of 'excess savings' (W_t), which households gradually spent down after reopening.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A large temporary flow (S_t) builds a higher wealth stock (W_t) that remains available to finance elevated consumption in later periods.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Macroeconomic Trade-off of Foreign Capital Inflows Cushioning U.S. Deficits
questions.prompt_template: In U.S. data, gross private domestic investment (FRED: GPDI) has persistently exceeded national saving when net government saving (FRED: TGDEF) is deeply negative, bridged by foreign purchases of U.S. securities (NCI > 0). What is the primary long-run trade-off of relying on foreign capital inflows to cushion crowding out?

hints.text: Consider both the immediate benefit to domestic interest rates/investment and the counterpart in net exports and future income flows.
Remember NCI = -NX, and foreign bondholders must be paid interest in future years.

options_template.text: Foreign capital inflows eliminate the federal deficit so the Treasury no longer needs to issue bonds.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financing-as-Elimination Fallacy): Foreign investors buy Treasury bonds, financing the deficit rather than erasing it.

options_template.text: Foreign inflows moderate the rise in U.S. real interest rates and reduce domestic investment crowding out, but at the cost of a wider trade deficit (NX < 0) and higher future interest payments to foreign bondholders.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Positive NCI cushions domestic capital formation today, but by accounting identity corresponds to NX < 0 and creates ongoing debt-service obligations to foreign lenders.

options_template.text: Foreign capital inflows force domestic physical investment (GPDI) to fall below domestic national saving.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Identity Sign Error): Positive NCI allows domestic investment to exceed national saving (I = S + NCI > S), not fall below it.

options_template.text: Foreign capital inflows raise U.S. real interest rates higher than they would be in a closed economy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Closed-vs-Open Rate Effect): Adding foreign savers expands the supply of loanable funds, keeping r* lower than it would be in a closed economy.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Critiquing a Causal Claim About Trade Deficits and National Saving
questions.prompt_template: A financial commentator points to the identity S - I = NX and argues: 'Because the United States has a trade deficit (NX < 0), this proves that reckless domestic undersaving caused the trade deficit.' Why is this causal conclusion incomplete?

hints.text: Recall the 'Clear It Up' distinction between an accounting identity and a causal mechanism.
Think about an alternative causal story starting from strong foreign investor demand for U.S. financial assets.

options_template.text: Because S - I = NX is mathematically false whenever a country has a flexible exchange rate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Identity-Rejection Error): S - I = NX holds ex post by national accounting definition under any exchange-rate regime.

options_template.text: Because a trade deficit implies S > I rather than S < I.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inequality Reversal): When NX < 0, S - I < 0, which means S < I (national saving is less than domestic investment).

options_template.text: Because S - I = NX is an ex post accounting identity; strong foreign demand for U.S. assets (or a domestic investment boom) could independently drive capital inflows (NCI > 0), appreciate the dollar, and widen the trade deficit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. An accounting identity shows what must balance after the fact, not which shock initiated the adjustment; strong U.S. investment opportunities or global safe-haven demand can drive NCI > 0 and NX < 0.

options_template.text: Because government budget deficits are excluded from national saving S.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (National-Saving Omission): National saving S = S_p + S_g explicitly includes public saving (budget deficits or surpluses).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating Broad Index ETFs Against Financial System Tasks
questions.prompt_template: A first-time saver invests $500 in a broad S&P 500 index ETF with an annual expense ratio below 0.05%. Which statement accurately evaluates what this financial intermediary accomplishes and what risk remains?

hints.text: Separate firm-specific (idiosyncratic) risk from economy-wide (market) risk.
Low-cost index funds slash transaction costs and idiosyncratic risk, but all 500 firms still face macroeconomic recessions.

options_template.text: It achieves near-complete diversification of firm-specific (idiosyncratic) risk at minimal transaction cost, but it cannot eliminate economy-wide market risk during a recession.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Pooling $500 across 500 corporations removes individual-company failure risk cheaply, while leaving the investor exposed to systematic downturns affecting the entire market.

options_template.text: It eliminates all investment risk—both firm-specific and economy-wide—guaranteeing positive returns every year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Risk Diversification Myth): Diversification across 500 stocks eliminates idiosyncratic risk, not systematic macroeconomic risk.

options_template.text: It counts directly as $500 of physical investment (I) in GDP because the ETF owns shares in productive corporations.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Secondary-Market GDP Error): Buying ETF shares transfers ownership of existing equities and is household saving (financial investment), not physical investment I.

options_template.text: It reduces liquidity compared with owning a single private startup because ETF shares cannot be sold on secondary markets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Liquidity Inversion): Exchange-traded funds trade continuously on secondary markets and are far more liquid than private startup equity.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Analyzing the March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank Liquidity Run
questions.prompt_template: In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) failed after holding large portfolios of long-term fixed-rate U.S. Treasury bonds funded primarily by uninsured, instantly withdrawable tech-startup deposits. Which two chapter mechanisms combined to trigger SVB's collapse?

hints.text: Connect what rising interest rates do to existing long-term bond prices with the bank's liquidity-transformation mismatch.
Remember the inverse relationship between bond prices and interest rates alongside sudden digital deposit withdrawals.

options_template.text: Rising interest rates raised the market value of SVB's long-term bonds, causing depositors to withdraw funds to avoid capital gains taxes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Bond-Price Direction Error): Rising interest rates lower—not raise—the market price of existing fixed-rate bonds.

options_template.text: The U.S. Treasury defaulted on its bonds, wiping out SVB's assets despite zero interest-rate changes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Credit-vs-Interest-Rate Risk Confusion): U.S. Treasuries did not default; SVB suffered interest-rate (duration) market-value losses combined with a liquidity run.

options_template.text: SVB held too much cash and too few long-term assets, preventing it from meeting depositor withdrawals.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Liquidity-Buffer Inversion): Cash is the most liquid asset; SVB failed because its assets were locked in rate-sensitive long-term bonds while its liabilities were instantly withdrawable.

options_template.text: Rising interest rates lowered the market value of SVB's long-term fixed-rate bonds (inverse bond-price effect), and rapid withdrawals of uninsured liquid deposits created an acute liquidity mismatch.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher market yields caused steep unrealized losses on long-duration bonds, and when uninsured depositors withdrew rapidly, SVB had to sell depressed bonds at a loss, triggering insolvency and a run.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting the Shift in 10-Year TIPS Real Yields (DFII10) from 2020-2021 to 2024-2026
questions.prompt_template: Between 2020-2021 and 2024-2026, the 10-year TIPS real yield (FRED: DFII10) moved from roughly -1.0% to around +1.8% to +2.1%. How does the loanable-funds investment hurdle model explain why residential and commercial real estate slowed while AI infrastructure investment continued?

hints.text: Compare the higher real borrowing hurdle (DFII10) against the expected rates of return across different sectors.
Only projects whose expected real return exceeds the higher real interest rate remain profitable.

options_template.text: Real estate developers borrow at nominal rates (DGS10), whereas AI firms borrow at zero interest.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Segmented-Market Fallacy): Both sectors face higher real borrowing costs when benchmark real yields rise; the difference lies in their expected rates of return.

options_template.text: The roughly 3-percentage-point jump in the real interest rate raised the profitability hurdle, screening out lower-margin housing and commercial real estate projects while high-expected-return AI and semiconductor projects still cleared the hurdle.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A higher real interest rate allocates scarce loanable funds toward capital projects with the highest expected returns while crowding out marginal, lower-yield projects.

options_template.text: A negative real yield (-1.0%) in 2020-2021 meant borrowers had to pay a penalty to invest, which discouraged construction.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative-Real-Rate Misinterpretation): A negative real interest rate makes borrowing exceptionally cheap in inflation-adjusted terms, encouraging—not discouraging—investment.

options_template.text: Higher DFII10 values shift the investment demand curve rightward for real estate and leftward for technology.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-vs-Shift & Direction Error): A higher real interest rate causes a movement upward along investment demand, screening out lower-return projects first.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Large Federal Deficits (FYFSD) Coincided with Low Real Yields in 2009 but High Real Yields in 2023-2026
questions.prompt_template: During the 2009 Great Recession, U.S. federal deficits (FRED: FYFSD) exceeded $1.4 trillion while 10-year TIPS real yields (FRED: DFII10) fell below 1%. In contrast, during 2023-2026, large structural deficits coincided with DFII10 rising above 2%. Which contrast from the three crowding-out regimes best explains this empirical divergence?

hints.text: Match 2009 and 2023-2026 to the slack/accommodation regime versus the full-employment upward-sloping supply regime.
In 2009, idle resources, weak private investment demand, and Federal Reserve accommodation kept real rates low; in 2023-2026, the economy operated near full capacity.

options_template.text: In 2009 the United States was a closed economy with vertical saving supply, whereas in 2023-2026 it became an open economy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Regime-Reversal Error): Vertical supply in a closed economy would have produced sharply higher real interest rates in 2009, the opposite of what happened.

options_template.text: Deficits cause crowding out only when nominal deficits exceed $1.5 trillion, so $1.4 trillion in 2009 was below the threshold.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Arbitrary-Threshold Fallacy): Crowding-out severity depends on economic slack, saving elasticity, and monetary accommodation—not an arbitrary dollar cutoff.

options_template.text: In 2009, deep economic slack, depressed private investment demand, and accommodative Federal Reserve policy corresponded to the flat/elastic supply regime (minimal crowding out), whereas 2023-2026 full-employment capacity constraints produced classic partial crowding out with higher real yields.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under severe recessionary slack and monetary accommodation (Panel c), deficits need not spike real rates; at full employment (Panel b), structural deficits compete directly with private borrowers and push r* up.

options_template.text: In 2009, the federal government financed its deficit by raising income taxes above G, eliminating public borrowing.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Contradictory Premise): By definition, a $1.4 trillion deficit means G exceeded net tax collections by $1.4 trillion.
