questions.topic: Policy Comparison: Saving vs. Investment Incentives
questions.title: Contrasting Retirement Saving Tax Incentives and Investment Tax Credits
questions.prompt_template: Policymakers want to boost long-run physical capital accumulation (I*). Compare Policy A (expanding tax incentives for household 401(k)/Roth IRA saving, holding the budget balance fixed) with Policy B (enacting a business investment tax credit, holding the budget balance fixed). How do their equilibrium effects differ?

hints.text: Identify which curve shifts under Policy A (supply S) versus Policy B (demand I).
Both policies raise equilibrium investment Q*, but they move the equilibrium real interest rate r* in opposite directions.

options_template.text: Both policies increase equilibrium physical investment (I*), but Policy A lowers the real interest rate (r*) by shifting S rightward, whereas Policy B raises r* by shifting I rightward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Encouraging household saving expands loanable-funds supply (r* down, I* up), while subsidizing business capital expands investment demand (r* up, I* up).

options_template.text: Both policies raise both r* and I* because any tax incentive increases government spending.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform-Rate-Effect Error): Holding the budget balance constant, a rightward supply shift lowers r* rather than raising it.

options_template.text: Policy A lowers I* because households spend less on consumption, whereas Policy B raises I*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Run Paradox-of-Thrift Misapplication): In the long-run loanable-funds model, higher saving lowers r* and finances higher physical investment I*.

options_template.text: Policy A raises r* and lowers I*, whereas Policy B lowers r* and raises I*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Complete Shift Reversal): This reverses the direction of the supply shift under Policy A and the interest-rate effect under Policy B.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Identifying When Fiscal Crowding Out Is Most Severe
questions.prompt_template: Under which combination of macroeconomic conditions will a $100 billion deficit-financed increase in government purchases cause the largest crowding out of private physical investment?

hints.text: Review the three reasons why crowding out is normally partial: elastic domestic saving, foreign capital inflows, and recessionary slack/Fed accommodation.
Crowding out is largest when all three cushioning channels are absent.

options_template.text: During a deep recession with high unemployment, an accommodative central bank, and open international capital markets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Minimal-Crowding-Out Conditions): Slack, central bank accommodation, and foreign capital inflows all cushion real interest rates and minimize crowding out.

options_template.text: In a small open economy with highly elastic foreign capital inflows and highly interest-sensitive domestic saving.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elastic-Supply Cushion): Highly elastic domestic and foreign saving absorbs the deficit with little rise in r* and little drop in private investment.

options_template.text: When private investment demand is completely vertical (insensitive to real interest rates).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inelastic-Demand Misinterpretation): If private investment demand were completely insensitive to r, higher real interest rates would crowd out zero private investment.

options_template.text: At full employment in a closed economy where domestic private saving is highly inelastic (nearly vertical) and private investment is sensitive to real interest rates.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Without economic slack, foreign capital inflows, or interest-responsive domestic saving, the deficit drives r* up sharply and displaces nearly a full $100 billion of rate-sensitive private investment.

questions.topic: Inflation Surprises, Fisher Parity & Bond Duration
questions.title: Impact of an Unexpected Inflation Surge on Long- vs. Short-Maturity Bondholders
questions.prompt_template: Suppose expected inflation jumps unexpectedly by 3 percentage points, pushing nominal market interest rates up across all maturities according to the Fisher relationship. Comparing a pension fund holding 20-year fixed-rate Treasury bonds with a saver holding 3-month Treasury bills, who suffers the larger immediate percentage market-price loss, and why?

hints.text: Combine the inverse bond-price relationship with how maturity (duration) affects sensitivity to interest-rate changes.
Longer-maturity fixed-rate bonds lock in below-market payments for many years, so their present discounted value drops much more sharply when i rises.

options_template.text: The 3-month Treasury bill holder suffers a larger percentage price loss because short-term bills mature too quickly to earn higher yields.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Duration Reversal): Short-term bills mature quickly, allowing the holder to reinvest at the new higher nominal rate almost immediately with minimal price decline.

options_template.text: The 20-year bondholder suffers a much larger percentage price loss because locking in fixed payments over a long horizon gives the bond higher duration and far greater price sensitivity to rising nominal yields.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher expected inflation raises nominal yields (i approx r + pi^e); because long-maturity bonds discount distant fixed cash flows at the higher yield, their market price falls much more sharply than short-term bills.

options_template.text: Neither bondholder experiences a market-price decline because U.S. Treasury securities have zero default risk.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Default-Risk vs. Interest-Rate-Risk Confusion): Even default-free Treasury bonds experience substantial market-price drops when nominal interest rates rise.

options_template.text: Both bondholders gain in market value because higher inflation increases the face value printed on fixed-rate bonds.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (TIPS-vs-Fixed-Rate Confusion): Standard fixed-rate bonds have a fixed nominal face value; only inflation-indexed bonds (TIPS) adjust principal for inflation.
